title: Finding the mass of a cart

stimulus.title: Finding the mass of a cart
stimulus.html:
Students want to find the mass M of a lab cart without using a balance. The cart sits on a level, low-friction track. A light string tied to the cart runs over a light, frictionless pulley at the end of the track to a hanger, on which they can place slotted masses. The total hanging mass m is known.

Their results (use g = 9.8 m/s²):

Hanging mass m (kg)Acceleration a (m/s²)1/m (kg⁻¹)1/a (s²/m)
0.0500.5820.01.724
0.1001.0810.00.926
0.1501.556.70.645
0.2001.975.00.508
0.2502.334.00.429

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe a procedure the students could use to collect the acceleration data in the table. Include the equipment used to measure each quantity and a way to reduce experimental uncertainty.

rubric.point: Measures the cart's acceleration with a named instrument: a motion detector (slope of the v-t graph), or a meterstick and stopwatch (a = 2d/t² from rest), or photogates
accept: motion detector at the end of the track; velocity-time graph slope gives a
time the cart from rest over a measured distance d with a stopwatch: a = 2d/t²

rubric.point: Varies the hanging mass m (known slotted masses on the hanger) and releases the cart from rest each time
accept: changes m for each trial, releasing from rest

rubric.point: Reduces uncertainty: repeats each trial several times and averages, or uses a range of at least five hanging masses
accept: three or more trials per mass averaged

parts.sample: Place a motion detector at the far end of the track, aimed at the cart. Put a known mass m on the hanger, hold the cart at rest, then release it. Record the cart's velocity against time with the detector and take the slope of the straight part of the v-t graph as a. Repeat each mass three times and average the slopes. Repeat for five different hanging masses from 0.050 kg to 0.250 kg.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: For the cart-string-hanger system, Newton's second law gives a = mg/(M + m). Indicate what quantities the students should plot to obtain a straight line, and explain how they can use the line to find M.

accept: m/a against m with slope 1/g and intercept M/g

rubric.point: Explains: the slope is M/g, so M = g × slope
accept: for m/a vs m: M = g × intercept

parts.sample: Take reciprocals: 1/a = (M + m)/(mg) = (M/g)(1/m) + 1/g. A graph of 1/a (vertical) against 1/m (horizontal) is a straight line with slope M/g and vertical intercept 1/g. So M = g × slope.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Plot the linearized data on the grid. Label the axes with the quantities and units, choose a linear scale, and draw a best-fit line.

rubric.point: Axes labeled with quantities and units: 1/m (kg⁻¹) horizontal, 1/a (s²/m) vertical
accept: both axes have a label and a unit

rubric.point: Linear scales that use most of the grid, with the five points plotted correctly
accept: evenly spaced tick marks; points in the right places

rubric.point: A single straight best-fit line (not connect-the-dots) with points scattered close to it
accept: one ruler-drawn line through the trend

parts.sample: Horizontal axis: 1/m (kg⁻¹), 0 to 20 in steps of 2. Vertical axis: 1/a (s²/m), 0 to 1.8 in steps of 0.2. The five points (4.0, 0.429), (5.0, 0.508), (6.7, 0.645), (10.0, 0.926), (20.0, 1.724) lie close to one straight line, drawn with a ruler, crossing the vertical axis near 0.11 s²/m.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass M of the cart using your best-fit line.

rubric.point: Finds the slope of the best-fit line from two points on the line (not data points unless on the line), about 0.081 kg·s²/m (accept 0.075 to 0.087)
accept: slope = rise/run from the drawn line, with units

rubric.point: M = g × slope ≈ 0.79 kg (accept 0.74 to 0.85 kg, consistent with the slope found)
accept: multiplies the slope by 9.8 m/s² and reports kg

parts.sample: Two points on the line: (4.0 kg⁻¹, 0.430 s²/m) and (20.0 kg⁻¹, 1.727 s²/m). Slope = 1.297 ÷ 16.0 = 0.0811 kg·s²/m. M = g × slope = 9.8 m/s² × 0.0811 kg·s²/m = 0.79 kg.
